newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil soybean prices to stay firm in 1997 - Safras.
newsitem.headline: Brazil soybean prices to stay firm in 1997 - Safras.

text.p: Prices for Brazilian soybeans and soy products are likely to remain above average this year, although below 1996 levels, based on strong world demand and the abolition of a state export tax, Safras e Mercado said.

"Although at levels well below 1996, this year can still be seen as favourable for Brazilian soybean producers, even taking into account normal weather in South America and the next U.S. harvest," the independent consultants said in a weekly report.
Among a list of supportive factors, Safras cited low worldwide stocks as demand outpaced growth, especially in Asia.
Meanwhile, a rise in U.S. demand would help sustain South American premiums at five to 10 percent above average.
Safras was basing its analysis on a previous forecast of a total Brazilian soybean crop of 26.28 million tonnes in 1996/97, up from a revised 23.49 million tonnes in 1995/96.
Barring any drops in the South American or U.S. crop, soybean prices should remain firm at $6.80 to $7.30 per bushel until April, when the new crop hits the market.

"From April onwards and with good weather in the U.S., prices would fall back below these levels if the tendency was confirmed of a new increase in planted area," Safras said. "But they would still remain above the 10-year average of $6.08."
In the internal market, the rise in the domestic crop was seen causing a drop in imports, although purchases of Paraguayan soybeans should remain high.
Meanwhile, the abolition of the ICMS state export tax in late 1996 would squeeze margins for crushing and was likely to boost overseas sales of soybeans to record levels, Safras said.
In a previous report, Safras forecast Brazil would export 5.8 million tonnes of soybeans in the 1997/98 marketing year (February/January) compared to 3.6 million in 1996/97.
It also predicted a high volume of forward sales, although these would start to lose pace once the harvest started.
"The tendency is for lower price fluctuations, a shorter gap between harvests (even with good prices) and a gradual market improvement from May onwards," Safras said.

Internal prices were seen at 10 to 15 percent above the historical average but would start to show weakness in January ahead of the start of harvesting in the north of Mato Grosso at the end of the month and in the west of Parana in February.
Soymeal and soyoil were seen following a similar pattern in 1997, with the focus on the abolition of the ICMS tax.

"In view of the importance of this item in the composition of internal prices, great changes can be expected in the dynamic of the market and everyone will take part in a learning process," Safras said.
Before, soybeans were subject to a 13 percent tax, soymeal 11.1 percent and soyoil an eight percent tax.
The level of crushing was likely to drop, even with a 12 percent rise in the harvest. But a drop in global stocks should keep the domestic soymeal market at 10 to 20 percent above average.

Soyoil prices should start to rise in January, reflecting a drop in the global production of other vegetable oils. With consumption set to hit record levels, this paved the path for soyoil to perform better than both soybeans and soymeal in 1997.
